deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Gauss's working sheet for the orbit of Vesta, discovered by Olbers on 29 March 1807. The page does two jobs: (A) it reduces his own micrometer observation of 6 April against a comparison star and tabulates all observed places from 29 March to 8 April; (B) it computes the Sun's place and equatorial rectangular coordinates for 29 March and 2 April from solar tables. The next folio does the same for 6, 3 and 8 April. These are the routine inputs for Gauss's orbit method (Theoria Motus).

(A) Observation of 6 April 1807.
- The clock is 8'41" slow on mean time ('Uhr zurück gegen M.Z.').
- Four sets of clock times (U.Z.) are given: 7h54'8", 8h5'26", 8h20'15", 8h32'0".
- Each set has micrometer transit readings in seconds: star 0|105, 0|38, 0|103, 0|26; planet 367.3|460, 331|429, 363|461, 325|421.
- My reconstruction: star midpoints are 52.5, 19, 51.5, 13 s. Planet midpoints are 413.65, 380, 412, 373 s.
- The differences are 361.15, 361.0, 360.5, 360.0, mean about 360.7 s of mean time.
- Times 1.0027379 (mean to sidereal) gives about 361.7-361.8 s, i.e. 1°30'26"-27". This matches the adopted RA difference Δα = +1°30'27.10".
- The declination difference Δδ = −7'11.23" presumably comes from the chord lengths. The pairs 404|498 and 407|493 are not explained on the page; I do not reconstruct them.

Comparison star:
- Catalogue place for 1800: α = 180°45'21.0", δ = 12°37'52.5".
- Precession to the date in 1807: +5'33.2" in α and −2'25.4" in δ. My check: over about 7.25 years with m + n sin α tan δ ≈ 46.0"/yr and n cos α ≈ −20.05"/yr, this gives +333.5" and −145.4".
- Mean 1807 place: 180°50'54.2", 12°35'27.1".
- Nutation: +17.49" in α, −6.81" in δ. Aberration: +15.77" in α, +8.62" in δ.
- Apparent star place: 180°51'27.46", 12°35'28.91".

Vesta:
- α = 180°51'27.46" + 1°30'27.10" = 182°21'54.56" ≈ 182°21'54.6".
- δ = 12°35'28.91" − 7'11.23" = 12°28'17.68" ≈ 12°28'17.7".
- The epochs are given as M.Z. 8h22'45" (for α) and 8h33'43" (for δ).
- Margin notes read 'Subtr. von d. Decl. 14"9' and a residual −1.9. Their exact use (refraction or parallax?) is not explicit.

Table of observed places with residuals against a provisional ephemeris (heading illegible):
- 29 March: α observations 29.6" and 39.8" are averaged to 184°8'34.7". δ = 11°47'23.7".
- 30 March: α = mean of 38.3, 32.9, 39.3 = 183°54'36.8". For δ, 35.0" is adopted out of 14.9" and 35.0".
- 1 April: α = mean of 27.2 and 9.8 = 183°27'18.5". δ = mean of 40.8 and 56.8 = 12°4'48.8".
- 2-8 April: single values, e.g. 6 April 182°21'31.2", 12°28'23.3"; 8 April 181°56'32.6", 12°36'7.8".
- Residuals (obs − comp) are of a few arcseconds.

(B) Sun's place from tables (Zach/Delambre type).

29 March:
- Mean longitude = epoch including the hours (9s9°11'27.71" + 22'29.67") + 1s28°9'11.48" (59 days, Jan+Feb) + 28°35'1.57" (29 days).
- Sum: 366°18'10.43" ≡ 6°18'10.43".
- The five perturbation-argument columns are summed mod 1000 in parallel: 7408.11, 701, 655, 679, 297.
- Equation of centre +1°55'23.09", then −1.37": L = 8°13'32.15".
- Small equations −7.14, −10.50, +8.43, +37.21 (sum +28.00) give true L = 8°14'0.15".
- Radius vector R = 0.9993129 − 111 − 10 − 18 (units of 10^-7) = 0.9992990. log R = 9.9996955.
- Obliquity 23°27'52.88" − 2.78" (nutation) = 23°27'50.10".
- Logs: log cos L = 9.9955005; log R cos ε = 9.9622122; log sin L = 9.1559596; log R sin ε = 9.5997651.
- Equatorial solar coordinates:
  - X = R cos L = 0.9889993
  - Y = R sin L cos ε = 0.1312719
  - Z = R sin L sin ε = 0.0569803

2 April:
- Mean longitude = 9s9°33'57.38" + 2s28°42'29.72" (90 days) + 1°58'16.66" (2 days) = 10°14'43.76". Argument sums: 7517.66, 837, 661, 689, 297.
- +1°55'24.40" − 1.38" gives 12°10'6.78". Corrections −6.40, −10.51, +8.39, +37.20 give L = 12°10'35.46".
- R = 1.0004684 + 191 − 23 − 1 = 1.0004851. log R = 0.0002106.
- Logs: log cos L = 9.9901179 (written; transcribed 9.9990179); log R cos ε = 9.9627273; log sin L = 9.3241264; log R sin ε = 9.6002802.
- X = 0.9779767, Y = 0.1935770, Z = 0.0840246.
errors: Arithmetically, all additions I checked are correct: star reduction, Vesta place, mean-longitude sums, argument columns mod 1000, radius-vector corrections, logarithms, and X, Y, Z for both dates.

The reduced 6 April place on this page (182°21'54.6", 12°28'17.7") differs from the 6 April entry in the table below it (182°21'31.2", 12°28'23.3") by about 23" in α and 5.6" in δ. The page does not show the reconciliation; perhaps a reduction to a common epoch, or the 14.9" correction. Unresolved.
The epochs M.Z. 8h22'45" and 8h33'43" could not be reproduced from the listed clock times plus the 8'41" clock correction. Their derivation is implicit.
Not a Gauss error: in the March 29 argument rows the second line has only four entries, the last column being blank. Otherwise 284+…≠297; with the blank, 284+0+9+4 = 297 correctly.

results.what: Differential micrometer reduction of a planet against a comparison star, with precession, nutation and aberration applied to the star, and mean-to-sidereal conversion of the transit-time difference.
results.modern_name: Differential astrometry; reduction from mean to apparent place

results.what: Sun's true longitude and radius vector from solar tables (mean longitude + equation of centre + planetary and lunar perturbations), then equatorial rectangular coordinates X = R cos L, Y = R sin L cos ε, Z = R sin L sin ε via logarithms.
Compilation of Vesta observations 29 March – 8 April 1807 with residuals against a provisional orbit, as input to Gauss's first Vesta orbit.
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Vesta orbit 1807, Monatliche Correspondenz; Theoria Motus methods)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine numerical reductions (star place, Sun coordinates) for Gauss's well-documented 1807 Vesta orbit work. They contain no new method, though they add working detail to a known episode.

checkable.asserts: Star RA 1800 plus precession equals the 1807 RA.
The apparent RA of the star is correct.
The apparent declination of the star is correct.
Vesta RA on 6 April equals star RA plus the difference.
Vesta declination on 6 April is correct.
The micrometer transit differences, converted to sidereal time, reproduce ΔRA = 1°30'27".
Mean solar longitude for 29 March is 6°18'10.43".
Mean solar longitude for 2 April is 10°14'43.76".
The table entries correspond to 29 and 59 days of mean solar motion (as I read the day counts).

transcription_corrections: Under Sonnenort April 2, '9,9990179' should read 9,9901179 (log cos L = 9.990118).
In the March 29 argument rows, the second line '10,43. 13. 1. 1.' has its last column blank; the four entries fill the first four columns.
'1 30 27,10' in the star reduction is the planet−star RA difference +1°30'27.10", not a further correction.
The heading 'Aneutheuses' is an uncertain reading; it heads the table of observed Vesta places (29 March – 8 April).
'Subtr. von d. Decl. 14"9' (subtract 14.9" from the declination) is a margin note beside the declination reduction.
